sections.text:
Paul left Titus on an island and gave him a job. “I left you in Crete”, he writes, to put things in order and “appoint elders in every city”. Titus is a short letter to a coworker who has been handed a hard assignment.

He is to appoint elders of proven character, correct teachers who cause trouble, and teach each group in the church how to live. But the letter does not rest on rules alone. Twice it reaches back to what God has done. First, “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men”, and it teaches people to live well. And God saved us, the letter says, not because of what we had done but “according to his mercy”. Good conduct in Titus grows from that gift.

Titus was a Greek and a trusted helper of Paul, mentioned in Galatians and 2 Corinthians. The letter is one of the three Pastoral Letters and shares their questions of date and authorship, which many scholars debate.

The letter shows the link between belief and conduct: sound teaching produces a good life, and a good life gives the teaching credit. Its instructions to different groups, including slaves, are read with the same care as the household passages in Ephesians and Colossians. Christians ask how far these words belong to their own time and how far they still speak, and the letter's own ground, the grace that has appeared, is where most readers begin.
